content: The respiratory rate, also known as the respiration rate, refers to the number of breaths a living being, such as a human, takes per minute. Research on monitoring respiratory rate is limited, with studies primarily focusing on issues such as the inaccuracy of respiratory rate measurements and its utility as a marker for respiratory dysfunction. In humans, respiratory rate is typically measured while the individual is at rest. This involves counting the number of breaths over one minute by observing the rise and fall of the chest. Respiratory rates can increase due to fever, illness, or other medical conditions. When assessing respiratory rate, it is also crucial to note whether the individual experiences any difficulty breathing. However, inaccuracies in respiratory rate measurement have been documented in the literature. For instance, one study found significant differences in respiratory rates when measured over a 15-second period compared to a full minute. In children under five years of age, measurements taken over 60 seconds showed the least variability compared to shorter periods. Another study observed that respiratory rates in infants, when counted using a stethoscope, were 20% to 50% higher than rates counted without a stethoscope from beside the cot. Similar discrepancies have been noted in animals, where handling them versus not handling them caused significant changes in their breathing patterns, likely due to the invasiveness of touch. Normal respiratory rates in healthy adults vary depending on the source, with reported ranges including 12 to 20 breaths per minute, 10 to 14 breaths per minute, or 14 to 18 breaths per minute. Given the relatively slow rate, it is recommended to count breaths over a full minute for accuracy. A systematic approach to deep breathing, such as complete yoga breathing, has been shown to lower respiratory rates in cardiac patients. This method involves slow, deep breathing at a rate of approximately six breaths per minute. In one study, cardiac patients practicing this technique for an hour daily over a month demonstrated slower breathing rates, higher blood oxygen levels, and improved performance on exercise tests. Average respiratory rates by age are as follows: Newborns: approximately 44 breaths per minute Infants: 20 to 40 breaths per minute Preschool children: 20 to 30 breaths per minute Older children: 16 to 25 breaths per minute Adults: 12 to 20 breaths per minute Respiratory minute volume refers to the volume of air inhaled or exhaled from a person's lungs in one minute. The diagnostic value of respiratory rate as an indicator of respiratory dysfunction has been investigated, but findings suggest its utility is limited. For example, one study found that only 33% of individuals presenting to an emergency department with oxygen saturation below 90% had an increased respiratory rate. In infants under six months, respiratory rate was not found to be a reliable indicator of illness severity. Approximately half of the infants studied had a respiratory rate above 50 breaths per minute, raising questions about the validity of using a cutoff of 50 breaths per minute as a marker for serious respiratory illness. Factors such as crying, sleeping, agitation, and age significantly influence respiratory rate, further complicating its use as a reliable indicator of serious illness. Consequently, the value of respiratory rate as a marker for severe illness is considered limited.
